messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Aleksander Nowak is a 21-year-old Polish-American man who works for a faith-based social ministry organisation and who, until several months ago, had considered his work the most meaningful thing in his life. He is married, newly so, and his wife had supported his decision to deploy as a relief worker to an active conflict zone in the Middle East, believing as he did that the work was urgent and necessary. What happened there has made it difficult for him to believe in urgency, necessity, or much else.

Aleksander had been stationed at a distribution point near a contested urban corridor. The work was logistically complex and emotionally demanding, but he had felt capable. Then, during what began as a routine supply handoff, a firefight erupted in the street adjacent to the compound. He was on the ground when the shooting started, surrounded by colleagues and civilians. People around him were screaming — in Arabic, in English, in languages he could not identify — and he had pressed himself against a concrete wall for what felt like hours but was, he was later told, approximately eleven minutes. A man he had been working alongside was struck and fell within his line of sight. Aleksander could not reach him. He remained pinned, certain he was about to die, listening to the shouting grow closer and then recede. When it was over, he was physically unharmed. He was evacuated within forty-eight hours and returned to the United States two weeks later.

The months since have been disorienting in a way he struggles to articulate. The memory of those eleven minutes does not feel like something that ended. When he tries to describe it to his wife — which he has done only twice, haltingly — the terror returns as fully as it was present in that corridor, and he has stopped trying. He had once assumed that surviving something meant, eventually, being on the other side of it. He has come to feel that no such other side exists for him. The memory carries a quality that unsettles him perhaps more than anything else: it is so extreme, so unlike anything in his prior twenty-one years of life, that he sometimes cannot fully accept it as his own history. It feels simultaneously unreal and inescapable.

His days are shaped by a vigilance that follows him into ordinary spaces. At his ministry office, where he now works primarily with resettlement cases, he finds himself scanning the room when colleagues raise their voices. A co-worker who gestured sharply during a meeting last month sent Aleksander's body into an immediate state of alarm that took the rest of the afternoon to subside. When clients who are Arabic-speaking become animated or distressed and raise their voices, he has begun excusing himself from those meetings, telling his supervisor he needs a moment, though he has not explained why. His work with refugee families — people who have fled the same kinds of violence he briefly witnessed — has become both more fraught and more isolating. He feels he cannot tell them what he carries, and he cannot pretend he does not carry it.

At home, he stays up well past midnight most nights, finding the transition to sleep intolerable. When he does sleep, he wakes in the dark and lies still, listening, checking. His wife has noticed and has asked. He has deflected. He has also begun declining the small pleasures she proposes — a dinner with friends, a film she thought he would enjoy — not because he is indifferent to her but because he has come to feel that allowing himself to feel hopeful or happy would be a kind of lie, or perhaps a vulnerability he cannot afford. He spends a portion of most evenings turning over the sequence of events from that day, tracing the decisions and contingencies, wondering what might have changed the outcome for the man who fell.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation at work in which a colleague casually mentioned a news story about military operations in the region. Aleksander left the room, sat in a bathroom stall for twenty minutes, and then called the ministry's employee assistance line. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping, though he said it quietly, is that it isn't.
